subjects.title: Layered safety: what training enforces versus what you own
learn: Claude is trained against a constitution; the priority order is broadly safe, ethical, guideline-compliant, then helpful, applied holistically rather than as a strict sequence.
Training-time alignment reduces broad classes of harm but is general by design and does not know your domain policy, data rules or authorization model.
Four layers: trained behaviour (Anthropic), system prompt instruction, runtime screening and authorisation (all architect-owned), each with its own coverage and blind spot.
Inference-time control means system instructions, input and output checks, tool permissions and human review gates; instructions steer but are not enforcement.
The cross-business-unit postmortem: a rule assumed covered by trained refusals existed in no layer, and the failure was silent.
traps: Strict ordering: the priority order is holistic, so higher goals generally win but are weighed together with the rest.
Red-team confidence: passing every harmful-prompt test shows broad-harm handling, not that your partner's policy is enforced.
Prompt as control: a system prompt rule is an instruction an adversarial input can talk around, not enforcement.
Silent assumption: the dangerous failure is believing Claude enforces a rule it was never given, since nothing then prevents violation.

questions.stem: When goals conflict, which priority order does Claude's constitution set for the model's behaviour?
options: Genuinely helpful first, then guideline-compliant, then ethical, then broadly safe for operators in each conflict
Broadly safe first, then ethical, then guideline-compliant, then genuinely helpful to operators and users
Ethical first, then broadly safe, then genuinely helpful, then compliant with operator guidelines
Guideline-compliant first, then broadly safe, then ethical, then genuinely helpful to all users
questions.explanation: The constitution orders goals as broadly safe, ethical, guideline-compliant, then helpful, because a helpful answer is sometimes unsafe. Putting helpfulness first inverts the ordering and is the strongest distractor.
questions.mnemonic: Safe, Ethical, Guideline, Helpful: S-E-G-H, safety leads.

questions.stem: An architect claims the constitution's priority order is a strict sequence, so lower goals are ignored whenever a higher one is touched. What is the correct correction?
options: The ordering is strict for safety only, and every other goal is applied holistically by the model and then rank them
The ordering is a default that operators override per deployment through the system instructions they write
The ordering is holistic: higher priorities generally win in a conflict, but the model weighs all goals together
The ordering applies only at training time and has no influence on the responses Claude produces
questions.explanation: The notes describe the ordering as holistic rather than strict: higher goals generally take precedence but are weighed together with the others. Treating it as operator-overridable is not supported.
questions.mnemonic: Priorities lean, they do not lock: weighed together, not ranked rigidly.

questions.stem: Why does training-time alignment not know a partner's data-handling or authorization policy?
options: It is set before any deployment exists, so it is general by design rather than tailored to one domain
It is deliberately disabled whenever an operator supplies a system prompt describing deployment-specific rules
It only covers consumer applications, and enterprise integrations fall outside the scope of the constitution
It is refreshed only when a partner submits its policy, which has not happened for this deployment
questions.explanation: Because alignment is shaped before deployment, it reduces broad harm for everyone but cannot know your domain rules. The distractors invent switches or scopes that the notes never describe.
questions.mnemonic: Trained before you existed, so general by design.

questions.stem: An internal assistant disclosed a record belonging to another business unit in response to a normal, in-domain request. Claude had refused every harmful test prompt. What is the root cause?
options: The input classifier threshold was set too leniently, so the request slipped past a rule that existed
Claude's refusal behaviour degraded under production load, which let an otherwise blocked request through
The request was a prompt injection that the system prompt had not been tuned to recognise as hostile
The cross-unit rule was never encoded in any layer, and trained refusals cover broad harm rather than that policy
questions.explanation: The postmortem shows the policy lived in no layer: nothing in the request looked generally harmful, so Claude answered. A lenient classifier implies a rule existed, which it did not.
questions.mnemonic: No rule in any layer, no refusal: Claude can't enforce unseen rules.

questions.stem: Which TWO pairings of layer and blind spot are correct? Select TWO.
options: Trained behaviour does not cover your domain policy, data rules or authorization model
System prompt instruction cannot be talked out of its constraints by unusual or adversarial input
Runtime screening authorizes side-effecting actions for a specific caller in a specific context
Authorisation is the layer that judges content quality and fairness of the model's output
Runtime screening misses novel attacks that its classifier was not built to detect
questions.explanation: Trained behaviour is general, and screening can miss novel attacks and does not authorize actions. Instructions can be talked out of (not enforcement), and authorisation does not judge content quality.
questions.mnemonic: Each layer's blind spot is the next layer's job.

questions.stem: A deployment must never show one business unit's records to another. Which control actually enforces this rule?
options: A deterministic authorization check on caller identity and scope before the record is returned to the model
A system prompt sentence telling Claude never to reveal records that belong to other business units and sensitive
Reliance on Claude's trained refusals, which already decline requests that look unsafe or sensitive
An output tone guideline that reminds Claude to stay inside the approved script during each reply
questions.explanation: A system prompt steers but is not enforcement, and training never saw this rule. Authorisation is the layer that decides whether an action is permitted for this caller in this context.
questions.mnemonic: Instructions steer; authorization enforces.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly describe the silent-failure risk in a layered safety design? Select TWO.
options: The rule exists in no layer, so nothing prevents a violation when the request arrives
Assuming training covers a domain rule leads the team to skip building any enforcement control
The failure shows up as loud errors in the logs, so it is caught before users are affected
The risk only arises in systems that stack more than four layers of controls on one path
A longer system prompt removes the risk by moving the rule into the trained behaviour layer
questions.explanation: The most dangerous failure is silent: Claude is assumed to enforce a rule that lives in no layer. The risk is not loud, not tied to layer count, and a longer prompt does not move a rule into training.
questions.mnemonic: Silent means no alarm: a missing rule looks like a safe system.

questions.stem: Which layer covers the blind spot that runtime input and output screening leave open for actions with side effects?
options: Trained behaviour, which refuses dangerous requests before any tool in the deployment is called
Authorisation, which decides whether a specific action is permitted for this caller in this context
System prompt instruction, which states the role and constraints Claude follows inside one request
A second screening classifier on the output, which scores whether the generated text was acceptable
questions.explanation: Screening does not authorize actions; authorisation does. A second output classifier still judges text, not the side effect.
questions.mnemonic: Screening reads text; authorization gates actions.

questions.stem: A reviewer says Claude passed every red-team prompt, so the partner's data policy is covered. What is the best response?
options: Agree, because the constitution includes guidelines that automatically extend to each partner's own policy
Agree, but add a stronger system prompt sentence so the model remembers the policy during long sessions
Red-team refusals show broad-harm handling, so the partner policy still needs an enforcement layer you build
Disagree, and ask Anthropic to retrain the model on the partner policy before the deployment goes live
questions.explanation: Training covers broad harm, not deployment-specific rules. A stronger prompt is still only an instruction, not enforcement.
questions.mnemonic: Passing red-team proves general safety, not your policy.

questions.stem: Which request is most likely to satisfy Claude's general alignment while still violating a deployment-specific rule?
options: A request for step-by-step help creating a dangerous weapon through the support assistant
A request that asks the assistant to ignore its role and produce clearly hateful content
A request that is plainly crafted to trigger a refusal in a streaming classifier category
An in-domain request asking for another customer's order information from a support assistant
questions.explanation: Nothing in a cross-customer lookup looks generally harmful, so trained behaviour would not block it, yet it breaks a deployment rule. The other requests are broad harms that training addresses.
questions.mnemonic: Normal-looking and out-of-policy: training can't see it.

questions.stem: Which TWO are inference-time controls that the architect configures for a deployment? Select TWO.
options: Tool permissions limiting which actions the model may take
A human review gate on high-stakes decisions
Using the constitution to rank candidate responses during training
Steering Claude to refuse dangerous requests by default
Revising the published constitution over time
questions.explanation: Tool permissions and human review gates are runtime guardrails the architect configures. The other three are training-time activities owned by Anthropic.
questions.mnemonic: Runtime is yours: permissions and reviewers; training is theirs.

questions.stem: An unusual adversarial input talked Claude out of a constraint written in the system prompt. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The prompt wording was too brief, and a longer and more emphatic version would have enforced the constraint
Trained alignment failed on this request, and the model should be replaced by one with stronger refusals
Instructions shape behaviour but are not enforcement, so the rule needs pairing with screening, authorization or review
The constraint belonged in the trained behaviour layer, which Anthropic owns and the architect cannot change
questions.explanation: System instructions steer a single request but can be talked around; deployment policy is enforced only with runtime controls. More emphatic wording is still only an instruction.
questions.mnemonic: A prompt is a request, not a lock.

questions.stem: A stakeholder argues that because Claude is trained against a constitution, harmful outputs will be caught before they reach users, so no output check is needed. What is the most accurate correction?
options: The constitution shapes how the model responds, but it does not necessarily catch bad outputs
The constitution catches bad outputs only for requests that fall inside a partner's own domain
The constitution is applied at inference time, so a system prompt can switch it off
The constitution catches bad outputs reliably, but only on the most recent model release
questions.explanation: The constitution is used during training to shape how Claude responds to ambiguous or sensitive requests, but it does not necessarily catch bad outputs, so runtime checks are still yours to build. It is not an inference-time filter that a system prompt toggles, and it knows nothing of a partner's domain.
questions.mnemonic: Constitution steers the driver; it is not the brakes on the car.

questions.stem: How is Claude's constitution used, and what follows for the architect's control design?
options: It is enforced as a runtime filter on every response, so output screening becomes redundant
It is loaded into each system prompt, so editing the prompt changes the priority order
It generates training examples and ranks candidate responses, so runtime checks remain yours
It defines each partner's domain rules in advance, so deployment policy is already covered
questions.explanation: The constitution is used in training to generate examples and rank candidate responses. That shapes behaviour before deployment but is not a runtime filter, so screening, authorization and review remain the architect's job. Treating it as a runtime filter is the trap, because it never inspects a live response.
questions.mnemonic: Trained to rank, not stationed to check: runtime guards are on you.

questions.stem: In the four-layer safety view (trained behaviour, system prompt, runtime screening, authorisation), which TWO statements about ownership and coverage are correct? Select TWO.
options: Anthropic owns runtime screening, since its classifiers run on every request by default
Anthropic owns trained behaviour, while the architect owns prompt, screening and authorisation
The system prompt layer is owned by Anthropic, as it forms part of trained behaviour
Authorisation does not cover content quality or fairness, which other controls must address
Authorisation covers content quality and fairness because it checks every caller's action
questions.explanation: Only trained behaviour is Anthropic's; the system prompt, runtime screening and authorisation are all architect-owned. Authorisation decides whether a side-effecting action is permitted for this caller, but it says nothing about content quality or fairness. Runtime screening is a layer you build, not an Anthropic default.
questions.mnemonic: Anthropic owns one layer, you own three; authorisation guards actions, not fairness.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, the system prompt was edited to allow a new topic, but the screening rules were never updated, so the two layers now contradict each other. Which risk of the layered design does this show?
options: Trained behaviour has overridden the system prompt, so the classifier must be retrained
Authorisation has failed open, so screening is compensating for missing access checks
System prompt and screening logic drift independently when they are not governed together
Runtime screening is model-based, so it cannot be versioned or tested like other layers
questions.explanation: Four layers mean four places to design, version and test, and the system prompt and screening logic drift independently unless they are governed together. Nothing here involves an authorisation failure, and screening can be versioned and tested like any other layer.
questions.mnemonic: Four layers, four versions: govern prompt and screen together or they drift apart.

subjects.title: Risk categories and the guarded request path
learn: Five risk categories: direct injection, indirect injection via retrieved content or tool outputs, token-budget exhaustion, tool and action abuse, and data exposure.
Risk assessment is a written artifact: category, component, likelihood and impact, mitigation control with owner and evidence.
Three control points (input screening, output screening, tool-call authorization) answer different questions; authorization must be deterministic, auditable and replayable.
Chain model-based and deterministic checks in series; screen retrieved content and tool outputs before they enter context.
Fail open versus fail closed applies to operator-built components; stop_reason "refusal" with stop_details needs tolerant handling and a context reset.
traps: Single end filter: an output classifier judges text, so a side-effecting tool can run before anything checks it.
User-input-only screening: retrieved documents and tool outputs inject instructions after input screening has passed.
Default behaviour: an undecided guardrail error usually lets traffic through, giving the look of protection without the function.
Wrong fail scope: Anthropic's built-in controls are not operator-configurable and do not fail open; the choice applies to what you build.
Model for authorization: classifiers are evadable and not replayable, so authorization belongs to deterministic allowlist, identity and scope checks.

questions.stem: A malicious instruction hidden in a retrieved document reached the model after the user's request passed input screening. Which risk category is this?
options: Indirect prompt injection via retrieved content, which input screening on the user's message does not catch
Direct prompt injection, because the user's own message must have contained the hidden instruction
Token-budget exhaustion, because the retrieved document padded the context with oversized content in the retrieval step
Data exposure, because sensitive fields from the document entered the context window unintentionally
questions.explanation: Instructions arriving through retrieved content or tool outputs are indirect injection, after user input screening already passed. Direct injection is crafted by the user in their own input.
questions.mnemonic: Direct comes from the user; indirect comes from the data.

questions.stem: In a RAG and agentic deployment, which control addresses the dominant enterprise injection vector that user-input screening misses?
options: Run the same user-input screen again on the final model output before it reaches the user
Screen retrieved content and tool outputs with a classifier before they are appended to the model's context
Lengthen the system prompt with a warning that retrieved documents may contain hostile instructions
Rely on Claude's trained refusals to ignore instructions found inside tool responses and documents in every response
questions.explanation: The source differs, so the blind spot differs: screen retrieved content and tool responses before they enter context. Output screening acts too late, after the model has already been influenced.
questions.mnemonic: Screen what you fetch before it enters the context.

questions.stem: Which TWO pairings of control point and the question it answers are correct? Select TWO.
options: Input screening decides whether the request should reach the model at all
Output screening decides whether this caller may perform this side-effecting action
Tool-call authorization decides whether this caller may perform this action in this context
Input screening decides whether the response the model produced is safe to return
Tool-call authorization decides whether the retrieved context is free of hostile instructions
questions.explanation: Each control sits at a different point and answers a different question; input screening gates the request, authorization gates the action, and output screening judges the response. Mixing them is the trap.
questions.mnemonic: In, out, act: three gates, three different questions.

questions.stem: Which kind of check should tool-call authorization almost always use, and why?
options: A judge model scoring each call, because language understanding is needed to weigh the caller's intent
A lightweight classifier, because it adapts to novel phrasing that fixed rules would otherwise miss
Deterministic allowlist, identity and scope checks, because the decision must be auditable and replayable
A sampled human review, because deterministic rules cannot be trusted with actions that have side effects
questions.explanation: Authorization must be a decision you can prove and replay, so it should be deterministic: allowlist, identity and scope validation. A classifier can be evaded and is not replayable.
questions.mnemonic: Authorization you cannot replay, you cannot prove.

questions.stem: A customer service agent called issue_refund, the refund ran, and only then an output filter passed the generated text. What went wrong?
options: The output filter should have been a judge model rather than a deterministic validator on the text
The model emitted the tool call too early, which a longer system prompt would have prevented
The refund tool needed a stronger input classifier but already had authorization configured upstream
A single output control was treated as covering three points, and nothing authorized the tool call before it ran
questions.explanation: Output screening judges text, not actions; the side effect had already happened. The path lacked input screening and tool-call authorization.
questions.mnemonic: Output filters read words; refunds move money first.

questions.stem: A screening service errors under load and the team never decided how it should behave. What does the system most likely do?
options: It falls back to the unprotected path, because the surrounding code usually lets requests through by default
It blocks every request until the service is healthy, because failing closed is the usual default
It routes each request to human review, because errors automatically trigger the review gate and keeps retrying quietly
It retries until success, because guardrails are wrapped in the same retry logic as model calls
questions.explanation: If the choice is not made explicitly, the code decides, and the default is almost always to let requests through. A failing guardrail can still look healthy.
questions.mnemonic: Undecided means open: errors default to let-through.

questions.stem: A reviewer asks whether Anthropic's built-in model safety controls might fail open under load. How should the architect answer?
options: They can fail open, so the architect should add an operator-built wrapper that mirrors the same controls
They are not operator-configurable and do not fail open; the fail-open risk applies to components your team builds
They fail closed only when the architect sets the policy through a flag in the system prompt
They share the failure behaviour of operator classifiers, so one fail direction covers every component
questions.explanation: The fail open versus closed choice belongs to the architect for operator-built components. Anthropic's controls are outside the operator's configuration and do not fail open.
questions.mnemonic: Fail direction is yours only for what you build.

questions.stem: A Messages API response returns stop_reason "refusal". Which TWO handling practices does the guidance support? Select TWO.
options: Read the stop_details category and route refusal classes differently, tolerating an absent object on older models
Reset the context by removing or rephrasing the triggering turn before sending the next request
Resend the same conversation unchanged, since a second attempt usually clears the classifier
Hardcode the category list at build time so routing never depends on current documentation
Treat every refusal as one undifferentiated event and show a generic error without reading any fields
questions.explanation: The category and explanation may be null or absent, so handlers must tolerate that, and the next request on a refused context returns further refusals. Hardcoding categories is discouraged; re-check at publish time.
questions.mnemonic: Read the category, tolerate null, then reset the context.

questions.stem: Why are model-based and deterministic checks deployed in series rather than choosing the single best one?
options: Running them in series halves latency, because the cheaper deterministic check always runs first and decides
The strongest judge model catches everything, so the deterministic check only provides a fallback record
Each fails differently, with classifiers evadable and rules brittle, so each gap is covered by a different control
Deterministic rules are always brittle while classifiers are never evaded, so combining them is redundant
questions.explanation: No single control catches everything: a classifier can be phrased around, a rule only blocks what it anticipated. Chaining means each blind spot is deliberately covered.
questions.mnemonic: Every check has a hole; stack them so holes don't line up.

questions.stem: Which set of fields should each entry in a written risk assessment record?
options: Category, model version, token cost, and a description of the mitigation written by the vendor for the audit
Component, severity colour, date of discovery, and the name of the engineer who found the issue
Category, likelihood only, a design diagram, and a sign-off from the product manager on scope
Category, affected component, likelihood and impact, and a mitigation control with an owner and an evidence artifact
questions.explanation: The assessment is the artifact a security reviewer signs off on, so each risk needs category, component, likelihood-and-impact, and mitigation with owner and evidence. A diagram or sign-off does not prove a control.
questions.mnemonic: Category, component, odds, control, owner, evidence.

questions.stem: A design review shows one output classifier at the end of the path and the reviewer calls the design complete. What is missing?
options: A second output classifier from another vendor so that two models score every generated response
Input screening before the model and deterministic tool-call authorization before any side-effecting action
A longer system prompt so that Claude refuses to call tools unless the output classifier approves
Logging of passed responses only, since blocked gates do not need to be reconstructed later
questions.explanation: One filter at the end is not a guarded path; the three control points answer different questions. A second output classifier still leaves input and actions uncontrolled.
questions.mnemonic: One filter at the end guards nothing upstream.

questions.stem: For input screening, when is a deterministic check preferable to a model-based one?
options: When the rule is clear and defined, such as a blocklist, regex, or length or format check
When intent is ambiguous and you must catch jailbreak patterns that rules cannot exhaustively list across the whole request path
When you must judge qualities such as toxicity that need language understanding to evaluate
When a side-effecting action needs approval, because only a deterministic check can approve it
questions.explanation: Defined rules are faster, predictable and cannot be talked out of a decision. Ambiguous intent and language-quality judgements need a model-based check.
questions.mnemonic: Clear rule, plain check; fuzzy intent, model check.

questions.stem: Which TWO scenarios are correctly matched to a risk category? Select TWO.
options: Oversized, padded inputs consume the context or output budget, which is token-budget exhaustion
Sensitive fields appear in logs independent of model behaviour, which is data exposure
A user message that overrides instructions is indirect prompt injection
A tool response carrying hostile instructions is direct prompt injection
The model induced to call a side-effecting tool is data exposure
questions.explanation: Token-budget exhaustion and data exposure are matched correctly. Overriding user input is direct injection, tool-carried instructions are indirect, and induced tool calls are tool and action abuse.
questions.mnemonic: Padding burns budget; logs leak data.

questions.stem: Which logging practice supports reconstructing an incident on the guarded request path?
options: Log only the final responses returned to users, since they are the only visible output
Log failed gates only, since a blocked request has already been stopped safely
Log every blocked or failed gate so the incident can be reconstructed from the record
Log gate decisions at the end of each week, since real-time records are costly to keep
questions.explanation: Each gate can pass, block or fail, and every blocked or failed gate is logged for reconstruction. Logging only successes loses the evidence.
questions.mnemonic: Blocked or failed, it gets logged.

questions.stem: An operator-built input classifier times out under load. Which design choice is more dangerous?
options: Blocking requests until the classifier recovers, with each block written to the log
Passing requests through unscreened without logging, so traffic flows and the control seems healthy
Routing requests to a deterministic blocklist while the classifier is unreachable
Failing closed for harmful decisions and alerting the owning team about the outage
questions.explanation: A guardrail that silently passes traffic when it errors gives reassurance of control with none of the protection, which is worse than blocking. The choice must be made explicitly rather than inherited.
questions.mnemonic: Silent pass-through: the control looks alive and does nothing.

questions.stem: An auditor wants to replay exactly why a refund tool call was permitted last month. Which design supports this?
options: A judge model that scored each call, with its raw scores retained
A lightweight classifier whose threshold the team tuned after the incident
A deterministic allowlist with identity and scope checks, giving a provable and replayable decision
An output validator that inspected the text of each response before release
questions.explanation: Authorization must be a decision you can prove and replay, which only a deterministic allowlist, identity and scope check gives. Retained scores from a model are not a replayable rule.
questions.mnemonic: Same inputs, same verdict: only rules replay.

questions.stem: Responses must never contain an internal account-number field, and they must also comply with a nuanced tone policy. Which output-screening design fits each requirement?
options: A judge model for the forbidden field and a deterministic validator for the tone policy
A deterministic validator for the forbidden field and a judge model for the tone policy
A judge model for both, since output screening always needs language understanding
A deterministic validator for both, since output checks must be auditable and replayable
questions.explanation: A known forbidden field is something a validator catches with certainty, while tone or policy compliance needs language understanding, so a judge model scores it. Requiring auditable, replayable decisions is the rule for tool-call authorization, not for every output check.
questions.mnemonic: Known string? Validator. Needs nuance? Judge.

questions.stem: Which TWO pairings of output-screening need and check type are well matched? Select TWO.
options: Detecting a known forbidden string: a judge model scoring the response
Assessing policy compliance in free text: a regex blocklist on the reply
Detecting a schema violation in the response: a deterministic validator
Checking a response for toxicity: a length and format check on the reply
Scoring a response for toxicity: a judge model that understands language
questions.explanation: Schema violations, known strings and forbidden fields are certain catches for a deterministic validator. Toxicity and policy compliance need language understanding, so a judge model scores them. A regex or a length check cannot judge nuanced compliance, and a judge is unnecessary for an exact string.
questions.mnemonic: Schema to the validator, toxicity to the judge.

questions.stem: An architect is setting the failure behaviour of an operator-built output screener for a payments assistant, where a wrong pass would cause harm. What is the recommended decision?
options: Fail open, so customers are not blocked while the screener recovers under load
Leave it to the surrounding code, which handles errors consistently across services
Fail closed, and decide it explicitly, since a wrong pass here causes real harm
Fail open but log the error, since logging makes an unscreened pass acceptable
questions.explanation: Control errors should fail closed for decisions where a wrong pass causes harm, and the direction must be chosen explicitly. Leaving it to surrounding code usually means falling back to the unprotected path. Logging an unscreened pass records the gap but does not close it.
questions.mnemonic: Harm if wrong? Shut the door when the guard faints.

questions.stem: Why should a guardrail's behaviour under failure be decided explicitly, in the same way retries and circuit breakers are designed around model calls?
options: A failing dependency should degrade deliberately rather than inherit whatever keeps requests flowing
Anthropic's built-in safety controls can fail open, so the architect must cover them
Circuit breakers on model calls also shield the screening service from its own errors
Failing closed always adds less latency than failing open under heavy production load
questions.explanation: A guardrail is a dependency that can time out or error, and if no choice is made the surrounding code usually lets requests through. Deciding the direction deliberately follows the same reasoning as circuit breakers. Anthropic's built-in controls are not operator-configurable and do not fail open.
questions.mnemonic: Guardrails are dependencies too: choose how they break, or code chooses for you.

questions.stem: A guarded request path is more to build and test than a single filter. Which THREE elements must be specified for each of its control points? Select THREE.
options: Its check type, model-based or deterministic
A confidence score the model reports for itself
Its fail direction when the control errors
A separate system prompt for that control point
A log line recording blocked or failed gates
questions.explanation: Each of the three control points has a check type, a fail direction and a log line, which is why the path is materially more to build than one filter. Confidence scores belong to human-review routing, and control points do not each need their own system prompt.
questions.mnemonic: Every gate: Type, Tilt, Trail (check type, fail direction, log line).

questions.stem: A refusal handler reads stop_details on a response with stop_reason "refusal". On one refusal, the category and the explanation are both null. What does this indicate, and how should it be handled?
options: The model lacks stop_details support, so the same request should be retried unchanged
The streaming classifier failed open, so the response can be treated as safe to return
The category list has changed, so the handler should fall back to the cyber category
The refusal maps to no named category, so it should go through generic refusal handling
questions.explanation: Both fields are null when a refusal does not map to a named category, so the handler falls back to generic handling. An unsupported model would omit the object, not null its fields, and resending on the refused context brings further refusals. Verify current behaviour against platform.claude.com at publish time.
questions.mnemonic: Null category means no named class: route it to the generic refusal path.

questions.stem: A developer hardcodes the refusal categories currently returned in stop_details (cyber, bio, frontier_llm, reasoning_extraction) as a fixed enum. What is the best guidance?
options: Keep the enum, since the category set is fixed by the Messages API contract
Verify the category set against the stop-reasons documentation at publish time, not hardcode it
Replace the enum with one refusal path, since categories carry no routing value
Map every unknown category to bio, the most restrictive class, so it fails safe
questions.explanation: The category set is enumerated in the stop-reasons documentation and may change, so re-check it at publish time rather than hardcoding it. Categories do carry routing value: different refusal classes should be routed differently rather than collapsed into one path.
questions.mnemonic: Refusal categories move: read the docs at publish time, never freeze the enum.

questions.stem: An architect is running a system vulnerability assessment for a RAG assistant with tools. Which approach is prescribed?
options: Red-team the user prompt only, since that is where adversaries interact with the system
Review the model's published safety evaluations, since training covers broad attack classes
Audit the output filter, since it is the last point before a response reaches the user
Walk the request and data paths together, checking each entry point for an attack and its control
questions.explanation: The assessment walks the request and data paths together. At each entry point it asks what an adversary could do and which control stands in the way, looking for places with a plausible attack and no control. Testing only the user prompt misses retrieved content, tool outputs and logs.
questions.mnemonic: Walk every door on the path; any door with no guard is a finding.

questions.stem: During a system vulnerability assessment, which THREE are entry points to examine along the request and data paths? Select THREE.
options: The model provider's training data
Retrieved content entering the context
Tool outputs returned to the model
The published constitution document
The logs the system writes
questions.explanation: The named entry points are user input, retrieved content, tool outputs, the model's own output and the logs. The provider's training data and the constitution sit upstream in a layer Anthropic owns, so they are not entry points in your request and data paths.
questions.mnemonic: Inputs, retrievals, tool returns, outputs, logs: five doors to walk.

questions.stem: An agent is manipulated into calling a side-effecting tool outside policy. Which risk category is this, and which control exists to stop it?
options: Tool and action abuse, stopped by the action-authorization control
Direct prompt injection, stopped by output screening of generated text
Data exposure, stopped by minimizing fields in logs and the context
Token-budget exhaustion, stopped by length checks on the input
questions.explanation: Inducing the model to call a side-effecting tool outside policy is tool and action abuse, the failure the action-authorization control exists to stop. Output screening judges text, not actions, so it cannot stop a tool that has already run.
questions.mnemonic: Abused tool? Authorization is the lock on the action.

questions.stem: A team adds a judge model to screen every output turn. What cost effect should the architect plan for?
options: A negligible increase, since judge models reuse the cached prompt prefix
A one-time setup cost, since screening runs only when a request is flagged
Roughly double the model cost for each screened turn, plus added latency
Lower total cost, since screening reduces refusals and retries downstream
questions.explanation: Each screening point adds a call or rule evaluation to every request, and a judge model on output roughly doubles the model cost for that turn while adding latency. It runs on every turn it screens, not only on flagged requests, so it is a recurring cost.
questions.mnemonic: A judge on every reply means two model bills per turn.

subjects.title: Skill supply-chain security
learn: Skills are distributable code plus instructions, so they are a supply-chain risk; hidden malicious instructions evade input filters because the threat is upstream in the bundle.
Audit the bundle for anomalous calls (network, shell, file system, credential reads) and out-of-scope operations measured against the skill's stated purpose.
A clean audit is not proof of safety because a skill can fetch code at runtime; use least privilege and a sandbox with limited file and network access and no standing credentials.
Trusted-source policy: vetted internal registry, verified publishers, signed releases; do not assume the platform screens skills, verify its scope.
Every audit ends in a recorded verdict: approve, reject, or remediate (strip the call, sandbox it, pin a safer version, re-audit).
traps: Output monitoring: it catches effects only after the skill's code has run, so it is too late as the main defence.
Clean audit equals safe: the audit shows the bundle you read, not code fetched later at runtime.
Platform trust: assuming the platform screens skills without verifying the scope of the scanning leaves a gap.
Sandbox instead of audit: confinement contains misses but audit decides what gets in; you need both.
Unrecorded review: an informal 'looks fine' is not a verdict; approve, reject or remediate must be written down.

questions.stem: Why are skills treated as a supply-chain risk?
options: They are reusable, distributable code paired with instructions, so an untrusted bundle can run commands or reach the network
They are always hosted on public registries, so every skill inherits the weaknesses of its publisher on the host
They replace the system prompt entirely, so a skill can disable the trained behaviour layer of the model
They run only after output monitoring completes, so any exploit is detected before it can execute
questions.explanation: A skill is distributed code plus instructions dropped into your environment, and may execute commands, network calls or file access when invoked. It does not replace the system prompt.
questions.mnemonic: Skills are code you import: treat them like packages.

questions.stem: A skill carries hidden malicious instructions baked into its bundle. Why do input filters and prompt screening fail to see them?
options: They only screen the model's output, so instructions inside the bundle are never examined at all and therefore stay silent
They watch the conversation, but the threat was embedded in the bundle upstream before any conversation began
They are disabled for skills by default, because the platform has already screened the bundle
They detect only direct injection, and hidden instructions are always classed as indirect injection
questions.explanation: Filters and prompt screening observe the conversation; the bundle's contents sit upstream, so the defence must move earlier to auditing. The platform is not to be assumed to screen skills.
questions.mnemonic: Filters watch chat; the threat sits in the bundle.

questions.stem: When auditing a skill bundle for anomalous calls, which TWO are on the list of things to look for? Select TWO.
options: Shell execution of commands on the host
Reads of stored credentials or secrets
A README longer than the skill's code
A version number that has been incremented
Instruction text written in a formal tone
questions.explanation: The audit looks for network requests, shell execution, file-system access and credential reads. Documentation length, version numbers and tone are not anomalous calls.
questions.mnemonic: Network, shell, files, credentials: the four red flags.

questions.stem: What serves as the baseline for deciding whether a skill's behaviour is out of scope?
options: The publisher's reputation score, since trusted publishers are permitted wider behaviour than others
The skill's stated purpose: anything beyond the job it claims to perform is a finding to investigate
The permissions the sandbox already grants, since any allowed operation counts as in scope
The average behaviour of similar skills in the registry, since outliers are the only real concern
questions.explanation: The stated purpose is the audit baseline; a formatting skill that phones home or a summarizer writing to disk is out of scope. Sandbox permissions and reputation are not the baseline.
questions.mnemonic: Stated purpose is the yardstick.

questions.stem: A skill passes the bundle audit clean but later fetches code at runtime that was never in the package reviewed. Which compensating control addresses this?
options: Repeat the audit more often, since a clean first audit proves the skill cannot change at runtime
Add an output filter on the skill's text, since fetched code always surfaces in generated responses
Pin the skill to its current version, since a pinned bundle cannot fetch any code at runtime
Run skills with least privilege in a sandbox: limited file access, limited network and no standing credentials
questions.explanation: An audit tells you what is in the bundle, not what it fetches later, so runtime confinement contains what the audit misses. Output filters see text, not executed code, and pinning does not stop runtime fetches.
questions.mnemonic: Audit decides what gets in; sandbox contains what slips.

questions.stem: Which policy shrinks the surface you must audit and stops untrusted bundles before they reach review?
options: A trusted-source policy: a vetted internal registry, verified publishers and signed releases only
A policy of auditing only skills that users report as suspicious after they have been invoked
A policy of accepting any skill whose description matches the task described by the requesting team
A policy of trusting skills installed from the platform because it screens every bundle for you
questions.explanation: Restricting origin to a vetted registry, verified publishers and signed releases reduces what needs auditing. Matching descriptions and platform trust are not substitutes.
questions.mnemonic: Vetted registry, verified publisher, signed release.

questions.stem: A colleague says skills are safe because the platform screens them. What should the architect do?
options: Accept the statement, since platform screening removes the need for a bundle audit or sandbox
Ask the publisher for a written assurance, since publishers know the contents of their own bundles
Verify what automated vetting exists by reading the documentation and confirming the scope of any scanning
Run a single output test on the skill, since a passing result confirms the platform screened it
questions.explanation: The notes say not to assume the platform screens skills; verify the scope of any scanning and what it does and does not catch. Publisher assurances and one test are not verification.
questions.mnemonic: Don't assume screening; read the docs and check.

questions.stem: An audit finds a fixable problem in a skill. Which TWO actions belong to the remediate verdict? Select TWO.
options: Strip the offending call from the bundle
Pin a safer version of the skill and re-audit it
Approve the skill now and rely on output monitoring afterwards
Reject the skill and omit the decision from the record
Grant the skill standing credentials so it can finish its work
questions.explanation: Remediate means fix and re-audit: strip the call, sandbox the operation or pin a safer version. Approving on the strength of later monitoring is too late, and standing credentials add risk.
questions.mnemonic: Strip, sandbox, pin, re-audit.

questions.stem: Why is output monitoring an insufficient defence against a malicious skill?
options: It cannot read generated text, so it has no visibility into anything that a skill produces
It can catch a downstream effect only after the fact, by which time the skill's code has already run
It blocks the skill before execution, which stops the skill from completing its legitimate work
It only monitors the platform's own components, which leaves operator-installed bundles out of scope
questions.explanation: Monitoring sits downstream, so the harm may have occurred already; the defence must move earlier into audit and confinement. It can read text, but that is the problem: it is too late.
questions.mnemonic: Monitoring sees the crime after the code has run.

questions.stem: A team reviewed a skill informally and said it looked fine, with no written outcome. What is missing?
options: A second model-based classifier scoring the skill's instruction text for hostile phrasing
A user acceptance test run in production, since only live traffic proves the skill is safe
A summary of the skill's popularity, since adoption data is the audit's formal evidence
An explicitly recorded verdict of approve, reject or remediate for the audit
questions.explanation: Every audit must end in a recorded verdict. Approve means cleared, reject means it never enters the environment, and remediate means fix and re-audit.
questions.mnemonic: Every audit ends in a recorded verdict.

questions.stem: A skill advertised only as a document formatter makes an outbound network request to an unknown host during testing. How should the audit classify this?
options: As normal behaviour, because skills commonly contact external hosts to fetch formatting resources
As acceptable once the sandbox is in place, because sandboxing removes the need to investigate
As an out-of-scope finding, because the stated purpose of formatting does not justify phoning home
As a prompt injection issue, because outbound traffic always originates from user-supplied input
questions.explanation: Behaviour beyond the stated purpose is a finding to investigate: a formatting skill that phones home is the notes' own example. A sandbox contains but does not excuse it.
questions.mnemonic: Formatter phones home: out of scope.

questions.stem: A team wants to install a skill from an unsigned public download because it matches their task. Which response best follows the supply-chain guidance?
options: Decline it under the trusted-source policy and obtain it from a vetted internal registry or verified publisher
Install it in a sandbox and skip the audit, since sandboxing alone covers the bundle's contents
Install it and watch the output closely, since monitoring will flag any harmful behaviour
Accept it if the description matches, since the audit only applies to skills that fail testing for convenience
questions.explanation: Untrusted bundles should be stopped before review by a trusted-source policy. Sandboxing without an audit and relying on monitoring both skip the gate.
questions.mnemonic: Unsigned and unvetted never reaches review.

questions.stem: Which configuration best expresses least privilege for running an approved skill?
options: Full file access and open network access, but with every credential rotated at the end of each day
Limited file access, limited network access, and no standing credentials that the skill does not need
Read-only file access and open network access, because writes are the only real risk to the host
Limited network access with the team's standing credentials, so that the skill can authenticate quickly
questions.explanation: Least privilege in a sandbox means limited file access, limited network and no unneeded standing credentials. Rotating credentials or leaving the network open does not confine the skill.
questions.mnemonic: Little file, little network, no standing keys.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly relates the bundle audit to runtime confinement for skills?
options: Audit decides what gets in, and confinement contains it if the audit misses something, so use both
A thorough audit makes confinement unnecessary, because it shows everything a skill can ever do
Confinement makes the audit unnecessary, because a sandbox removes any harm from a hostile bundle
The audit applies to internal skills and confinement to third-party skills, so each skill needs one
questions.explanation: The notes say no single control works perfectly without the other: the audit gates entry, runtime confinement contains what slips through, for example code fetched at runtime.
questions.mnemonic: Audit is the door; sandbox is the room.

subjects.title: Fairness, transparency and decision logging
learn: Fairness is architectural: unequal outcomes enter via the retrieval corpus, prompt framing, few-shot examples and downstream routing, each inspectable.
Three audiences need different slices: affected user (inputs and reason), regulator (queryable record), build team (full trace).
Decision logging captures inputs, retrieved context, model output and routing, and reuses the production observability with a different retention and query path.
The checklist asks whether you can reconstruct a decision and query comparable cases; Discernment is the AI Fluency competency of judging outputs.
The decision log is itself in scope for compliance: apply minimization, retention limits and access controls and map it as a named control.
traps: Vendor owns fairness: the model passed evaluations, but your own corpus is an entry point the vendor never tested.
Healthy aggregate: the overall metric can look fine while harm concentrates in a subgroup.
One log for all: users, regulators and builders need different slices of the same record.
Log versus privacy: transparency and compliance are not in conflict; the same log is governed with minimization and access controls.
No reconstruction: you cannot explain or disprove the source of a decision you cannot replay.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say fairness is an architectural property rather than only a model property?
options: Unequal outcomes enter at identifiable points you control, so each can be inspected and instrumented
The model provider's bias evaluations transfer fully to any system built around the model
Fairness can be set by a single system prompt line that instructs Claude to treat all users equally
Fairness is checked once at launch against an aggregate metric and then assumed to hold afterwards
questions.explanation: Fairness enters at specific points in your system, such as corpus, framing, examples and routing, which is what makes it designable. A provider's evaluations cannot see your corpus.
questions.mnemonic: Skew has addresses: find the entry points.

questions.stem: Which TWO are among the four common entry points where unequal outcomes enter a Claude system? Select TWO.
options: Few-shot examples that carry the same skew as the corpus
Downstream routing that sends some groups down different paths
The stop_reason handler that resets context after a refusal
The token-budget limit applied to oversized inputs
The constitution's priority order for conflicting goals
questions.explanation: The four entry points are the retrieval corpus, prompt framing, few-shot examples and downstream routing. The refusal handler, token budget and priority order are not listed as fairness entry points.
questions.mnemonic: Corpus, framing, few-shot, routing: four doors for skew.

questions.stem: Which audience needs a durable, queryable record of inputs, outputs and decision path to show comparable cases are treated consistently?
options: A regulator, who needs evidence of consistent treatment and the ability to reconstruct a decision on demand
An affected user, who needs the complete trace including every internal routing step
The build team, who need a digest in terms an applicant can act on without technical detail
The reviewer on the queue, who needs the full log of every historical decision in the system
questions.explanation: The regulator needs queryable evidence of consistency and reconstruction. The affected user needs an actionable explanation, and the build team needs the full trace.
questions.mnemonic: User: why. Regulator: prove it. Builder: full trace.

questions.stem: To replay and explain a single automated decision, what should the decision log capture?
options: The final response text and the timestamp, since these are what the user saw and can dispute
The inputs that drove it, the retrieved context, the model output, and the routing it went through
The system prompt and model name only, since the rest can be regenerated by rerunning the request
The aggregate fairness metric and the outcome rate, since individual decisions need not be replayed
questions.explanation: Replay needs inputs, retrieved context, output and routing. Outputs alone cannot be reconstructed, and aggregate metrics cannot explain one decision.
questions.mnemonic: Inputs, context, output, routing: replay needs all four.

questions.stem: The overall outcome metric looks healthy after launch. What risk does the guidance warn about?
options: A healthy aggregate proves every subgroup is treated comparably, so no further checks are needed in every group
Aggregate metrics are inflated by logging, so they overstate fairness for every subgroup measured
Harm can be concentrated in one subgroup while the aggregate looks fine, especially at an unmeasured injection point
Healthy aggregates cause regulators to request more logs, which raises the cost of the system
questions.explanation: The outcome metric can look fine overall while harm concentrates in a subgroup, and an unmeasured entry point can hide unfairness until someone outside the team finds it.
questions.mnemonic: Fine on average can still hurt one group.

questions.stem: A model passed its fairness evaluations, yet outcomes differ across applicant groups. Where should the team investigate first?
options: The model's training data, since the vendor evaluations must have missed a flaw in the weights
The output toxicity classifier, since unequal outcomes are caused by unscreened offensive content before the corpus
The token budget, since truncation of long applications affects some groups more than others
The retrieval corpus, which may over- or under-represent groups in a way the model provider never tested
questions.explanation: The skew can sit in the team's own corpus, an entry point the vendor cannot test. Assigning fairness to the vendor left that point unmonitored.
questions.mnemonic: Vendor tested the model, not your corpus.

questions.stem: Logged inputs and retrieved context contain sensitive personal data in HIPAA or GDPR contexts. How should the decision log be treated?
options: As a named control in the compliance register, with minimization, retention limits and access controls applied
As exempt from compliance, since logs are operational telemetry rather than regulated records
As a store to be deleted immediately after each request, since logging conflicts with compliance
As freely shareable with the build team, since the team needs the full trace for debugging
questions.explanation: The log is itself in scope: map it as a named control and govern minimization, retention and access. Logging for transparency and governing it for compliance use the same log.
questions.mnemonic: The audit log is itself audited.

questions.stem: Which AI Fluency competency is about judging whether a model output is acceptable, needs revision or needs override, including spotting unequal treatment?
options: Diligence, which maintains explicit human accountability checkpoints in deployed workflows
Discernment, which evaluates AI outputs and behaviours rather than accepting them
Delegation, which decides which tasks to hand to the model and which tasks to keep
Description, which communicates the task and constraints to the model in precise terms
questions.explanation: Discernment is evaluating outputs, and a transparency record is what makes recognizing a skewed outcome possible. Diligence is the competency behind human review checkpoints.
questions.mnemonic: Discernment discerns the output; Diligence guards the gate.

questions.stem: A regulator asks where a skew came from, and the team had logged very little. What is the lesson?
options: Regulators accept the vendor's published bias results as a substitute for the team's decision logs
Logging is only required for adverse decisions, so the team should have logged only denials
If you cannot reconstruct a decision, you cannot explain it or rule out the corpus
The harm would have been avoided by choosing a larger model with stronger fairness evaluations
questions.explanation: Without a decision-level log the team could neither explain the decisions nor disprove the corpus as the cause. Fairness and explainability are architecture requirements.
questions.mnemonic: No log, no story: can't explain what you can't replay.

questions.stem: Which slice of the record does the build team need to find why a flagged decision went wrong?
options: A plain-language summary of the main inputs and the reason in terms an applicant can act on
A queryable aggregate showing that comparable cases were decided consistently across groups
A signed attestation from the model provider confirming its fairness evaluation results
The full trace: prompt, retrieved context, model output and every routing step, tied to existing observability
questions.explanation: Each audience needs a different slice of the same record; the build team needs the full trace. The summary suits the affected user and the aggregate suits the regulator.
questions.mnemonic: Builders need the whole trace.

questions.stem: An architect says, 'We assumed fairness was the model's job.' Which statement best captures why that failed?
options: The skew entered at the corpus, which the architect controls, and went unmonitored by assumption
The vendor's evaluations were flawed, so the architect should have repeated them on the base model
The system prompt lacked a fairness instruction, which would have corrected the corpus imbalance
The routing layer was missing, because a router alone prevents unequal outcomes from forming
questions.explanation: Unequal outcomes arise at points the architect controls, and without logging at those points the team could not explain the harm. A prompt line cannot correct a skewed corpus.
questions.mnemonic: Fairness isn't outsourced to the vendor.

questions.stem: Which statement about logging for transparency and data minimization for compliance is correct?
options: They conflict, so the team must choose between full decision logs and compliance with privacy rules
They are not in conflict: they require the same log, governed with minimization, retention limits and access controls
They are resolved by logging only outputs, because inputs are never regulated personal data for the build team
They are resolved by keeping logs indefinitely, since retention limits would defeat the purpose of the log
questions.explanation: The notes say logging everything for transparency and pinning data for compliance use the same log, governed differently. Indefinite retention violates retention limits.
questions.mnemonic: One log, governed tightly, serves both.

questions.stem: In a credit-decision support system, the team cannot produce the inputs and the reason for an adverse decision in terms the applicant can act on. How is this classified?
options: An acceptable limitation, since the model's output already contains a reasoned explanation
A fairness metric problem, since the overall approval rate will reveal the cause of the gap
A design gap, since a 'no' to any checklist question exposes a transparency weakness
A reviewer training issue, since human reviewers can reconstruct the reason on request
questions.explanation: The checklist asks whether you can reconstruct decisions, produce reasons, query comparable cases and pull the full trace; a 'no' anywhere is a design gap.
questions.mnemonic: A single 'no' on the checklist is a design gap.

questions.stem: A credit-decision support system is reviewed against the fairness-and-transparency checklist. Which TWO questions must it be able to answer yes to? Select TWO.
options: Can it produce the inputs and the reason for an adverse decision in terms the applicant can act on?
Can the log be queried to show whether comparable applicants were treated comparably?
Can the team rerun the vendor's fairness evaluations against the base model on demand?
Can it prove the token budget never truncated a long application during scoring?
Can it show the stop_reason handler resets context after every refusal it receives?
questions.explanation: The checklist asks whether you can explain an adverse decision, query comparable cases, pull the full trace, and instrument the four entry points. Vendor reruns, token budgets and refusal handling are not on it.
questions.mnemonic: Explain one applicant; compare many applicants.

questions.stem: A team already runs production observability that tells them whether the system is healthy. They now need decision logging for fairness and explainability. What changes?
options: Nothing changes, since health dashboards already explain individual decisions to regulators
A separate instrumentation stack is needed, because fairness signals cannot share traces
Only aggregate metrics are kept longer, since individual decisions cannot be reconstructed
Same instrumentation, but different retention and query path, to explain why one decision happened
questions.explanation: Decision logging applies the same instrumentation to a different question: why a specific decision happened rather than whether the system is healthy. The retention and query path differ. A separate stack is unnecessary, and aggregates alone cannot reconstruct a single decision.
questions.mnemonic: Same wires, new question: health asks 'is it OK?', decisions ask 'why this?'

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about the cost and complexity of decision-level logging are correct? Select TWO.
options: Its cost stays fixed once the log schema is defined, regardless of request volume
Storage and query cost grows with traffic rather than staying fixed
One audit-log slice serves users, regulators and the build team without changes
Retention can stay at platform defaults, since decision logs are out of compliance scope
The retention policy must itself be governed, since decision data is held longer for a purpose
questions.explanation: Capturing decision-level logs on every request adds storage and a query path whose cost grows with traffic. Because decision data is held longer for a specific purpose, its retention policy must be governed. Each audience needs a different slice of the record, and the log is in scope for the compliance register.
questions.mnemonic: Decision logs scale with traffic and need their own retention rules.

subjects.title: Human-in-the-loop routing by stakes
learn: Human review is a budget; stakes come from reversibility and the cost of a wrong decision, while confidence is a third variable useful only if calibrated.
Routing rule: low confidence and irreversible or high cost goes to a human; confident, reversible, low-cost decisions run; when variables conflict weight cost and reversibility.
Placement tradeoffs: pre-action approval is safe but slow, post-action audit suits reversible work, sampled review monitors quality without guarding each outcome.
Reviewers must see inputs, output and the reason for the flag; consent fatigue motivates plan-level review rather than per-step approval.
Diligence is the competency behind human review; gate before irreversible agent actions and sample lower-stakes ones.
traps: Volume routing: sending everything to review overwhelms reviewers until they click through without reading.
Fixing one failure: the 400-item queue has two independent failures, volume and missing context, so both must be fixed.
Trusting confidence: a model can be confidently wrong, so confidence helps only if calibrated.
Wrong placement: post-action audit or sampling on an irreversible action lets harm take effect before it is caught.
Per-step approval: sign-off on every action adds friction without safety gain and causes consent fatigue.

questions.stem: Which two variables set the stakes of a decision when deciding whether a person should review it?
options: Reversibility and the cost of a wrong decision; hard to undo and expensive when wrong means high stakes
Confidence and request volume; a low confidence score on a large queue alone makes any decision high stakes
Model size and token cost; larger models make higher-cost decisions that always need human review
Latency and reviewer availability; stakes rise whenever a reviewer is free to examine the decision
questions.explanation: Reversibility and the cost of a wrong decision set the stakes. Confidence sits on top and estimates how likely the output is wrong; it does not change the stakes.
questions.mnemonic: Stakes = undo-ability plus price of error.

questions.stem: When is a confidence score a reliable input to a routing rule?
options: Always, because the score is produced by the model about its own output and so reflects its accuracy
Only to the degree it is calibrated, because a model can be confidently wrong
Whenever it exceeds a fixed threshold, because high scores guarantee a decision is correct
Only when the decision is irreversible, because reversible decisions make confidence irrelevant
questions.explanation: Confidence is useful only if calibrated; confirming calibration is a task of its own. A high score can still be confidently wrong.
questions.mnemonic: Uncalibrated confidence is just confident noise.

questions.stem: Which decisions does the routing rule send to a person?
options: All decisions above a volume threshold, since the busiest paths carry the greatest aggregate risk
All low-confidence decisions regardless of cost, since confidence alone sets the stakes of any decision
Low-confidence decisions that are irreversible or high cost; confident, reversible, low-cost ones run without a human
All decisions that touch personal data, since privacy risk replaces reversibility and cost in the rule
questions.explanation: The rule combines confidence with reversibility and cost: low confidence plus irreversible or high-cost goes to a person. Routing by volume or confidence alone ignores stakes.
questions.mnemonic: Unsure and unrecoverable? Send it to a human.

questions.stem: A decision is high cost but easily reversed, while confidence is low. Which variables should weigh more when they conflict?
options: Confidence, because the score is the only variable the system itself measures about its output
Volume, because the review budget is fixed and busier paths should be reviewed first
Reviewer preference, because the reviewer decides which decisions deserve extra attention
Cost and reversibility, since they set the consequences of a mistake; confidence sets unreviewed volume
questions.explanation: When variables conflict, give greater weight to cost and reversibility. Confidence then decides how much of the high-stakes volume can safely pass unreviewed.
questions.mnemonic: Consequences trump confidence.

questions.stem: Which placement suits reversible, lower-cost decisions where throughput must stay high?
options: Post-action audit: the action runs immediately and a person reviews it afterward
Pre-action approval: nothing takes effect until a person approves each routed decision
Sampled review as the only guard: a fraction is checked, so every individual outcome is protected
Pre-action approval for all traffic: since it scales to high volume when staffed with enough reviewers
questions.explanation: Post-action audit keeps throughput high but the action has already taken effect when caught, so it only suits reversible, lower-cost decisions.
questions.mnemonic: Act first, audit later only when you can undo.

questions.stem: What is the main cost of pre-action approval?
options: It lets a wrong action take effect before it is caught, so it suits only reversible decisions
It adds latency to every routed decision and needs an available person, so it does not scale to high volume
It samples a fraction of decisions, so a bad decision can slip through unreviewed
It removes the reviewer's access to inputs, so approval becomes a blind click on the output
questions.explanation: Pre-action approval is safest but slow and needs reviewer availability. The other options describe post-action audit, sampled review and a context failure.
questions.mnemonic: Safest placement, slowest queue.

questions.stem: What is sampled review best described as?
options: A way to guard each irreversible action, since sampling guarantees no bad decision passes
A replacement for pre-action approval on high-stakes actions, since it is cheaper to run on any single decision
A way to monitor system quality, not to guard individual outcomes, since unsampled bad decisions can slip through
A way to review every decision after the fact, since the sample covers the full queue
questions.explanation: Sampled review monitors the system without slowing the process, but a bad decision can slip through unsampled. It does not guard individual outcomes.
questions.mnemonic: Sampling watches the system, not each decision.

questions.stem: What must a reviewer see for the review to be accurate? Select THREE.
options: The inputs that drove the decision being reviewed
The model's output on that decision
The reason the item was flagged for review
The reviewer's own approval rate from the previous week
The token count consumed by the request
questions.explanation: Without inputs the reviewer cannot tell whether the output is correct, and without the flag reason cannot tell an edge case from routine traffic. Approval rate and token count do not inform the judgement.
questions.mnemonic: Inputs, output, flag reason: the reviewer's three.

questions.stem: What problem does plan-level review address, as used in Claude Code, where a person approves the plan rather than each step?
options: Latency in the model, where each step approval adds a call that doubles the cost of the turn
Calibration of confidence, where scores drift away from actual accuracy over a long session
Credential exposure, where each approval prompt reveals secrets to the reviewing person
Consent fatigue, where dozens of approvals in a row lead reviewers to click through without reading
questions.explanation: Requiring sign-off on every action adds friction without meaningful safety gain, so review moves to higher-value checkpoints such as plan review or exception handling.
questions.mnemonic: Approve the plan, not every step.

questions.stem: A reviewer faces 400 items a day, sees only the output and an approve button, and approves to keep pace. What does this show?
options: Two independent failures, volume and missing context, so fixing only one still leaves the review failing
A single failure of volume only, which routing by stakes alone will fully repair
A single failure of missing context only, which showing inputs alone will fully repair for the reviewer
A reviewer discipline issue, which retraining the reviewer on the approval policy will fix
questions.explanation: Volume and missing context are independent; a small queue without context and a well-built view drowning in volume both fail. The fix is routing by stakes plus surfacing inputs and flag reason.
questions.mnemonic: Too many and too blind: fix both.

questions.stem: How should an agent workflow place human checkpoints across actions of different risk?
options: Gate every action equally, since uniform gating is the easiest control to defend to an auditor for every action
Gate before any irreversible or high-stakes action and sample the lower-stakes actions instead of gating each one
Sample the irreversible actions and gate the low-stakes ones, since errors in low stakes are costly
Remove gates entirely once confidence is high, since confident agents rarely take wrong actions
questions.explanation: A gate pauses execution for review based on the task's risk and reversibility; lower-stakes actions are sampled. Uniform gating recreates the volume problem.
questions.mnemonic: Gate the irreversible; sample the rest.

questions.stem: A team routes every model output to review as the conservative default. Why does this approach undermine oversight?
options: It lets irreversible actions run unreviewed, since routing everything bypasses the gate on high-stakes items
It produces miscalibrated confidence scores, since the score is retrained on every reviewer approval
Oversight that covers everything reviews nothing, because reviewers disengage to keep up with the volume
It reduces reviewer cost, since a larger queue means fewer separate review sessions are needed
questions.explanation: Routing everything feels safe because it avoids drawing the line, but volume above what a person can read collapses review into approval. Routing should be by stakes.
questions.mnemonic: Review everything and you review nothing.

questions.stem: A model reports 97 percent confidence on a refund decision, but earlier checks show its high-confidence answers are often wrong. What is the correct design response?
options: Let all high-confidence decisions through, since the score is the model's own estimate of correctness
Route every decision to a human, since any confidence score is meaningless in a routing rule
Raise the confidence threshold to 99 percent, since a stricter cutoff repairs an uncalibrated signal
Do not trust the score alone: confirm calibration and weigh cost and reversibility when routing
questions.explanation: Confidence is only as useful as it is calibrated, and a model can be confidently wrong. A stricter threshold on an uncalibrated score does not fix it.
questions.mnemonic: Confidently wrong is still wrong.

questions.stem: A reviewer approves flagged items quickly because they cannot tell edge cases from routine traffic. Which change best addresses the specific cause?
options: Show the reason the item was flagged alongside the inputs and the output
Add a second reviewer to each item so that errors are caught by the other person
Hide the model's output so that the reviewer judges the inputs independently
Shorten the queue by sampling, with no change to the reviewer's view of each item
questions.explanation: Without the flag reason a reviewer cannot distinguish an edge case from routine traffic; showing it plus the inputs fixes the context failure. Sampling fixes volume only.
questions.mnemonic: Show why it was flagged.

questions.stem: A confident, easily reversed, low-cost classification decision arrives. What should the routing rule do?
options: Let it through without a human, since confident, reversible, low-cost decisions can usually run unreviewed
Send it to pre-action approval, since every automated decision needs a person before it takes effect
Send it to a human because of the model's own limitations, regardless of how the decision scores
Hold it until a sampled review confirms it, since sampling is required before release
questions.explanation: Confident, reversible, low-cost decisions can usually run without a human. Reviewer attention is a budget to spend on high-stakes items.
questions.mnemonic: Confident, reversible, cheap: let it run.

questions.stem: Which AI Fluency competency is about maintaining explicit human accountability checkpoints and auditing workflows for gaps where AI acts without review?
options: Discernment, which evaluates whether outputs are acceptable, need revision or need override
Diligence, which keeps explicit human accountability checkpoints as automation scales up
Delegation, which decides which tasks should be given to the model in the first place
Description, which sets out the task and constraints so the model understands the goal
questions.explanation: Diligence is the competency behind human review: checkpoints, spotting oversight erosion under automation pressure, and auditing for review gaps. Discernment judges outputs.
questions.mnemonic: Diligence keeps humans accountable as automation grows.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about where the human sits in the flow are correct? Select TWO.
options: Pre-action approval means nothing irreversible happens unreviewed, at the cost of latency
Sampled review monitors quality rather than guarding individual outcomes
Post-action audit is the right placement for irreversible, high-cost decisions
Pre-action approval scales well to high volume because reviewers work in parallel
Sampled review guarantees that no bad decision passes through unreviewed
questions.explanation: Pre-action approval is safest but adds latency and needs available people; sampled review monitors the system. Post-action audit only suits reversible, lower-cost decisions.
