questions.mnemonic: Approve before, audit after, sample to monitor.

questions.stem: A team says its decision log already makes high-stakes automated decisions safe, because every one can be explained afterwards. What is missing?
options: A longer retention period so explanations stay available to regulators
A routing rule that stops wrong decisions before they take effect
A sampled review of logged decisions, which guards each individual outcome
Re-instrumentation of the system, since logs cannot feed a reviewer view
questions.explanation: A log explains decisions after the fact, but it does not decide which decisions a person should weigh in on before they take effect. A routing rule does that. Sampled review monitors the system rather than guarding individual outcomes, and the existing log can feed the reviewer view without re-instrumenting.
questions.mnemonic: The log explains the crash; the routing rule stops the car first.

questions.stem: When designing the reviewer's view for routed decisions, how should the architect relate it to the decision log already in place?
options: Replace the log, since reviewer screens need their own separate instrumentation
Ignore the log, since reviewers should judge only the model's final output
Treat the log as raw material and decide what to surface from it and when
Rely on the log alone, since any logged decision can be explained afterwards
questions.explanation: The decision log is the raw material for the reviewer view, so the work is deciding what to surface and when, not instrumenting again from the start. Showing only the output fails reviewers, who also need the inputs and the flag reason.
questions.mnemonic: Don't rewire: mine the log you already have for the reviewer's screen.

questions.stem: Anthropic's research on agent autonomy (verify the current framing at publish time) found that sign-off on every action adds friction without meaningful safety gain. Which TWO practices does it favour instead? Select TWO.
options: Keep approval on every step, but give reviewers faster approve buttons
Have a person monitor what is happening and step in when needed
Remove the human role entirely once per-step sign-off has been dropped
Move review to higher-value checkpoints such as plan or exception review
Replace every pre-action gate, including irreversible ones, with sampled audit
questions.explanation: The research favours a person monitoring what happens and stepping in when needed, with per-step approvals reduced and review moved to higher-value checkpoints such as plan review or exception handling. That does not remove the human, and the exact design still depends on the workflow's risk.
questions.mnemonic: Watch and step in; review the plan and the exceptions, not every click.

subjects.title: Compliance obligations as controls with evidence
learn: Choosing a route that survives HIPAA, GDPR or FedRAMP is a pre-filter, not proof; a regulation states an outcome and you supply the control.
Every obligation needs three things: a technical control, a named owner and an evidence artifact (the most-missed element).

Mappings: HIPAA to BAA, admin setting and eligible features (security lead); FedRAMP to authorized route and record (platform owner); residency to regional config and data-flow record (data owner); transparency to decision log and sample reconstruction (architect).
Training use and retention are different claims; data excluded from training may still be retained or monitored.
Reviewers accept proof a control is live, not design documents; revalidate on a cadence because configurations drift.
traps: Route equals compliance: a compliant entry point is only a prerequisite for the controls, owners and evidence.
Design document as proof: reviewers accept a signed agreement, config screen, authorization record or log query, not a plan.
Training equals retention: excluded from training does not mean not stored, logged or monitored.
One-time mapping: configurations drift, so unrevalidated artifacts go stale and controls silently fail.
Residency copies: logs, caches and monitoring paths can write to a second region unless the data-flow record covers them.

questions.stem: A team chose a delivery route that survives HIPAA constraints and considers compliance settled. What is wrong with that conclusion?
options: The route is a prerequisite, not proof; each obligation still needs a control, a named owner and an evidence artifact
The route must be re-chosen yearly, since regulations replace the permitted routes each year
Compliance is the vendor's responsibility, so the team's only task is to keep the contract on file
Design documents are sufficient evidence once the route is chosen, so the register can be skipped
questions.explanation: Surviving the pre-filter yields an allowed route, but reviewers also ask who owns the control and what evidence shows it holding in practice.
questions.mnemonic: Route is the ticket, not the proof.

questions.stem: GDPR, HIPAA and FedRAMP state what must be true. What does the architect own as a result?
options: A policy statement, a project sponsor, and a risk rating for the quarterly steering meeting for the executives
A specific technical control, an accountable owner, and an evidence artifact showing the control is live
A vendor attestation, a legal reviewer, and a design document describing the intended controls
A model configuration, an escalation contact, and a training record for the engineering team
questions.explanation: Regulations state outcomes and leave the technical control to you, so each obligation becomes control, owner and evidence. Documents and attestations alone are not evidence of a live control.
questions.mnemonic: Control, owner, evidence: the compliance trio.

questions.stem: Which element of the control, owner, evidence triple is most often missed?
options: The technical control itself, since teams rarely implement anything for an obligation in each project
The named owner, since owners are always assigned only after the first audit finding
The evidence artifact that shows the control is live, which is what the reviewer checks
The framework reference, since teams rarely record which regulation applies to a control
questions.explanation: The notes stress always including the evidence artifact; a control no one can demonstrate is indistinguishable from one that is not running.
questions.mnemonic: No evidence, no control, as far as an auditor knows.

questions.stem: Which TWO items are evidence a reviewer accepts for the HIPAA obligation? Select TWO.
options: The signed Business Associate Agreement
The admin setting showing HIPAA compliance enabled, plus the eligible-feature list
A design document describing the intended HIPAA architecture
A statement that the model was trained without the data
The residency configuration showing the approved region
questions.explanation: For HIPAA the evidence is the signed BAA and the admin setting showing compliance enabled, plus the eligible-feature list; the owner is the security lead. Residency evidence belongs to a different obligation.
questions.mnemonic: BAA plus the switch plus the feature list.

questions.stem: For a US government workload at the required impact level, what do the technical control and evidence consist of?
options: Any compliant-looking entry point, plus the vendor's marketing statement on certification coverage
A regional configuration for the approved boundary, plus a data-flow record covering logs and caches
The decision log retained for the required period, plus a sample reconstruction of one decision in the register
An Anthropic-documented authorized route, plus its authorization record and confirmation that the workload runs exclusively on it
questions.explanation: FedRAMP maps to delivery through an authorized route with an authorization record and confirmation of exclusive use; the owner is the platform owner. The other options are residency and transparency evidence.
questions.mnemonic: Authorized route, authorization record, exclusive use.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports a data-residency obligation?
options: The residency configuration alone, since pinning processing to the approved region covers all copies
The residency configuration and a data-flow record showing where every copy lives, including logs, caches and monitoring
A signed Business Associate Agreement, since it states where data can be processed and stored
An authorization record for the delivery route, since the route determines where every copy lands
questions.explanation: Residency needs regional configuration and validation that logs, caches, monitoring and retention paths stay within the boundary; the owner is the data owner. Configuration alone misses secondary copies.
questions.mnemonic: Prove every copy, not just the main store.

questions.stem: A vendor says data is excluded from model training by default. What follows for the retention claim?
options: Retention is also off, since excluding data from training means that nothing is stored at all to the contract
Retention is limited to 30 days, since training exclusion implies a fixed short retention window
Nothing automatically; data may still be retained or monitored for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance or audit
Retention is irrelevant to compliance, since only training use of data is regulated by the frameworks
questions.explanation: Training use and retention are two distinct claims and must not be collapsed. The notes give no fixed retention window.
questions.mnemonic: Not trained on is not the same as not kept.

questions.stem: A security and legal reviewer asks for proof of a control. Which artifact do they accept?
options: A signed agreement, a configuration screen, an authorization record or a returned log query showing the control is live
A design document that names the control but lists no owner and no operating evidence
A diagram of the compliant entry point, annotated with the framework clause it addresses
A statement that the team intends to enable the control before the next scheduled audit
questions.explanation: Reviewers accept proof that a control is live, not design documents; a control no one can demonstrate looks the same as one that is not running.
questions.mnemonic: Show it live, not on paper.

questions.stem: Why must the compliance register be revalidated on a regular cadence?
options: Frameworks are rewritten annually, so each control must be redesigned to match the new text
Configurations drift and artifacts go stale, so a control true at design time can be false in production
Evidence artifacts expire automatically after one audit, so they must be regenerated every cycle
Owners change role regularly, so control ownership must be reassigned on each cycle
questions.explanation: Producing and maintaining evidence is ongoing work because configurations drift. The residency story shows a control that was real at design and silently false later.
questions.mnemonic: Configs drift; evidence must be re-proved.

questions.stem: Months after launch, a logging configuration began writing request metadata to a second region. Why was this not caught until audit?
options: The processing region was misconfigured at design time, so the control never matched the policy
The route was not authorized for regulated data, so the data should never have been in the region
No one owned the residency control, and no evidence artifact tracked where data was landing
The decision log was not retained, so the team could not reconstruct individual decisions
questions.explanation: The control was correct on paper, but with no owner or data-flow record nothing detected the change. A design document replaced evidence at audit time.
questions.mnemonic: No owner, no data-flow record, no alarm.

questions.stem: For the transparency obligation, what is the technical control and the evidence a reviewer accepts?
options: The retained, queryable decision log, with a sample reconstruction of one decision from the live log as evidence
The authorized delivery route, with an authorization record confirming exclusive use of that route
The regional configuration, with a data-flow record covering logs, caches and monitoring paths
The signed agreement, with an admin setting and a list of eligible features that remain in scope
questions.explanation: Transparency maps to decision logging retained for the required period, evidenced by a sample reconstruction; the owner is the architect.
questions.mnemonic: Reconstruct one decision from the live log.

questions.stem: The team's compliance mapping was written once at design time, with no owners and no logging wired to show controls operating. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: They chose the wrong delivery route, since a compliant route would have produced evidence automatically
They mistook surviving the pre-filter for establishing compliance, leaving controls unowned and unprovable
They documented too little detail, since a longer design document would have satisfied the reviewer
They lacked a regulator contact, since regulators confirm controls instead of the team's own evidence
questions.explanation: A compliant route is a prerequisite, not proof. Each obligation needs a control, a named owner and a living evidence artifact that is revalidated as the deployment changes.
questions.mnemonic: Passing the filter isn't passing the audit.

questions.stem: At audit, a reviewer asks for evidence that data stayed in-region and the team produces a design document. How will the reviewer treat it?
options: As sufficient, since a design document records the approved region and the intended pinning of processing in every scenario
As partly sufficient, since a design document counts once the owner signs it after the audit
As insufficient, since a control that no one can demonstrate is indistinguishable from one that is not running
As sufficient for residency only, since design documents are not accepted for HIPAA or FedRAMP
questions.explanation: Reviewers accept proof that a control is live, such as a configuration screen, authorization record or returned log query, and do not accept design documents alone.
questions.mnemonic: Design docs describe; evidence demonstrates.

questions.stem: Which pairing of obligation and owner matches the mapping?
options: HIPAA with the security lead, FedRAMP with the platform owner, and data residency with the data owner
HIPAA with the data owner, FedRAMP with the security lead, and data residency with the platform owner
HIPAA with the architect, FedRAMP with the data owner, and data residency with the security lead
HIPAA with the platform owner, FedRAMP with the architect, and data residency with the data owner
questions.explanation: The mapping assigns HIPAA to the security lead, FedRAMP to the platform owner, data residency to the data owner, and transparency to the architect.
questions.mnemonic: HIPAA security, FedRAMP platform, residency data.

questions.stem: Which practice best prevents a residency control from silently breaking after a configuration change?
options: Re-read the original design document each quarter to confirm the intended region has not changed
Rely on the delivery route's authorization record to guarantee that all copies stay in the region
Disable logging in non-approved regions only once an auditor has raised a specific finding
Name an owner and revalidate the data-flow record on a regular cadence to detect drift
questions.explanation: Configurations drift, so an owner and a living, revalidated evidence artifact are what catch a change. A design document or route record does not track where data lands.
questions.mnemonic: Owner plus cadence catches drift.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about training use and retention are correct? Select TWO.
options: They are two distinct claims that must not be collapsed into one
Data excluded from training by default may still be retained or monitored for abuse prevention or audit
Excluding data from training means the data is not stored or logged anywhere
Retention is regulated only when the retained data is also used for training
Retention is automatically capped at the same period as the training exclusion
questions.explanation: Training use and retention differ; data excluded from training may still be retained or monitored for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance or configured audit purposes.
questions.mnemonic: Not trained on is not the same as not kept.

questions.stem: In the mapping of compliance obligations to controls and owners, who owns the control that makes decisions reconstructable on demand?
options: The security lead, who owns the HIPAA control
The data owner, who owns the residency data-flow record
The platform owner, who owns the authorized route
The architect, who owns the retained, queryable decision log
questions.explanation: The cross-framework transparency obligation is met by the decision log from the fairness work, retained and queryable, and the architect owns it. The security lead owns HIPAA, the platform owner owns FedRAMP and the data owner owns residency.
questions.mnemonic: Who built the decision log owns its proof: the architect.
